label: Big bed or own room
countdownLabel: the first night in the big bed

what_happens.title: What happens with the big bed
goals: Moving to a big bed or own room is a growing-up step
The bedtime routine stays the same
what_happens.parentSkill: Keep the bedtime routine exactly the same; only the bed changes.

who_is_there.title: Who is close at night
goals: [[GROWNUP]] is close by in the house
The cuddly toy keeps me company
Siblings or pets may be nearby
who_is_there.parentSkill: Show your child exactly where you sleep and walk the path from their bed to your room together.

what_i_do.title: What I do in the big bed
goals: Stay in bed until the morning signal
Know the plan if I wake up
what_i_do.parentSkill: Use a simple morning signal, like a night light that changes colour, and agree the wake-up plan.

if_scared.title: If I feel scared at night
goals: The dark and night sounds can feel scary
Feeling lonely is normal at first
Calm tools: night light, toy, slow breaths, the plan
if_scared.parentSkill: Name the night fears without dismissing them: 'The dark can feel scary. Your night light is on, and I'm close by.'

rehearsal.title: Let's practise the big bed
goals: Try the bed for a nap or quiet time first
Set up the night light and toy
rehearsal.parentSkill: Do a daytime practice: quiet time in the new bed with a story, then a "pretend morning" celebration.

steps: Help set up the new bed or room
Choose the sheets, a night light and a cuddly toy
Do the usual bedtime: bath, pyjamas, teeth, story
Climb into the big bed and say goodnight
Stay in bed until the morning light or the clock says so
Call softly or walk to a grown-up if really needed
Wake up and celebrate the first night
sensory: a bigger bed that feels wide
new sheets with a fresh smell
house sounds in the night, like pipes or wind
honestyNotes: The first nights may include waking up, coming out of bed or feeling scared of the dark; never promise it will be easy or that the child will not feel lonely. Keep the bedtime routine the same. Never use the new bed as a punishment. Let the parent decide the rules about coming to their room.

questionButtons.text: What if I need the toilet at night?
fallbackAnswer: Go before bed, and a little light can show the way.
You can call [[GROWNUP]] to help.

questionButtons.text: Why do I need a big bed?
fallbackAnswer: You are growing, and a big bed has more room.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you why now is a good time.

questionButtons.text: Who will use my old bed?
fallbackAnswer: [[GROWNUP]] will tell you, maybe a baby brother or sister, or it gets stored.
Your big bed is all yours.

techniques.label: The same routine
techniques.how: Keep the bedtime steps exactly the same.

techniques.label: A night light
techniques.how: Let your child choose a soft night light.

techniques.label: A cuddly toy
techniques.how: A favourite toy stays in the bed all night.

techniques.label: Walking the path
techniques.how: Walk the path from the bed to your room in the light.

techniques.label: A morning signal
techniques.how: Use a wake-up light or clock as the morning signal.

techniques.label: One check-in
techniques.how: Offer one quiet check-in after goodnight, and always do it.

techniques.label: A room check
techniques.how: Check the room together with the light on.

techniques.label: A happy place
techniques.how: Picture a favourite place while falling asleep.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

ritual: Night light on, toy in my arms
Stay in bed until the morning light

pain: If your tummy feels worried, take a slow breath.
body: Go to the toilet before bed.

sensory: That is just the wind. Your night light is on.

strangers: Only our family is in the house at night.
separation: I will check on you once.

safety: You are safe in your big bed.

social: Lots of kids your age sleep in big beds.
love: I love you, even while we sleep.

sentences.text: Soon [[CHILD]] will sleep in a big bed, maybe in a new room.
It is a growing-up step that many kids take.
First [[CHILD]] helps set it up and chooses the sheets.
Then the bedtime routine stays the same: bath, pyjamas, teeth and a story.
Before bed, here is a story about a little fawn called Fern.
Fern used to sleep curled next to Mama Deer.
Now she was getting her own soft moss bed.
First Fern helped gather the softest moss.
Then she chose a glow-worm as her night light.
Next she did her bedtime steps: wash, cuddle, story.
Fern lay down in her new moss bed.
It felt big and a little strange.
Mama said, I am just over there, under the oak.
Fern hugged her toy acorn, and her eyes closed.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
Next [[CHILD]] climbs into the big bed with a cuddly toy.
A night light glows softly.
[[GROWNUP]] says goodnight, and the door can stay a little open.
Last, in the morning, there is a big celebration.
[[CHILD]] can choose the night light and the cuddly toy.

A branch creaked, and a shadow moved.
Fern called, Mama?
Mama came and lay down for a moment.
Mama did not say, there is nothing there.
Mama said, that was the wind in the branches, and the shadow is the oak.
You are safe, and I am close.

She thought of the sunny meadow where she loved to play.
Her eyes closed again.

Fern tucked her acorn in for the real night.

Fern felt ready.

Kids move to big beds or their own rooms at many different ages, and there is no right one.
Having your own space means you can choose how it looks and keep your things.
It takes most kids a week or two to sleep well in a new bed.
A consistent bedtime routine tells the brain it is time to sleep.
[[CHILD]] can design the room layout with [[GROWNUP]].
Knowing where everyone sleeps makes the house feel safe in the dark.
A quick check-in after lights out, done consistently, helps kids settle without needing to call out.
Some kids like a soft sound, like a fan or quiet music.
Pets in the room can be comforting, if the family allows it.
[[CHILD]] can agree a check-in time with [[GROWNUP]].
Everyone wakes up briefly several times a night; most people just do not remember.
Having a plan for waking up, like a breath, a sip of water and a change of position, helps you settle yourself.
Wake-up clocks that change colour make the rule easy to follow.
Using the toilet right before bed reduces night wakings.
[[CHILD]] can track good nights on a chart.
Fear of the dark is one of the most common fears in childhood and usually fades with time.
The brain is more alert to sounds at night because it is quieter.
Shadows can look like shapes; turning on the light to check can help once.
Listening to calm audio or practising slow breathing distracts the mind from worry loops.
[[CHILD]] can make a worry box and put worries in it before bed.
Starting with naps or quiet time in the new bed makes the night less of a leap.
Choosing bedding, a lamp and decorations builds ownership.
A predictable morning reward, like choosing breakfast, motivates staying in bed.
Sticking to the plan for a week usually builds the habit.
[[CHILD]] can pick the first-night celebration.
